paras: The threatened lynching of Doc Bacon took place at the jail in Boydton, Mecklenburg County, Virginia, on September 4, 1903, when a crowd from Chase City tried to stop the sheriff from removing Bacon, a Black man under sentence of death, after Governor Montague respited him for thirty days. An armed posse held the jail until Judge Homes persuaded the crowd to disperse, and Bacon was taken by special train to Petersburg. Papers across the country reported a narrow escape "both from the law and from a mob," and the Richmond Planet later printed an eyewitness account.

Bacon and Anderson Finch were convicted of an attempted criminal assault on Mrs. C. E. Geoghegan at Chase City in late July; Finch's confession implicated Bacon, who denied guilt. After Finch told a Petersburg jailer that Bacon was innocent, the governor briefly respited Bacon, and Finch was hanged alone at Boydton on September 2.

According to the Rev. J. B. Ferrell, who rode with Bacon from Petersburg, Commonwealth's Attorney E. C. Goode boarded the train and then telegraphed the governor that he was satisfied Bacon was not guilty.

At Boydton the last religious rites were under way when the governor's telegram granting a thirty-day respite arrived. Ferrell wrote that a "swarming crowd" outside shouted during the prayers for Bacon's neck to be broken, and the Times-Dispatch's correspondent reported that "considerable excitement existed" and the dispensary was closed as a precaution.

Late in the afternoon, when the sheriff and his deputies tried to take Bacon back to Petersburg, a large delegation from Chase City in front of the jail enclosure demanded that he not be removed. The sheriff summoned a heavily armed posse inside the jail, and for a time a clash seemed likely; Ferrell put the newly sworn deputies at about 25, armed with Winchesters. A dispatch in the St. Louis Republic added that "Lynch him!" was shouted repeatedly and that the crowd pressed around the officers demanding the prisoner.

Judge Homes, who had tried the case, spoke for fifteen or twenty minutes from the jail-office steps, promising that the sentence would finally be carried out. The crowd then dispersed, and at twilight Bacon was slipped out a side door to an engine and caboose that carried him toward Emporia and Petersburg.

No report of arrests among the crowd was found. On September 5 more than 200 Chase City citizens met in the town hall, where Judge Homes and Mayor T. D. Jeffress spoke against lynch law. The meeting resolved that Bacon's sentence should be enforced and implored the governor to act with care so that "good citizens" would not be forced to take the law into their own hands.

Goode told the Times-Dispatch that new witnesses could explain the chief circumstance against Bacon and that "of all lynching he regards a judicial one as the worst." Bacon was nevertheless hanged at Boydton on October 3, 1903, declaring his innocence on the gallows.

The Times-Dispatch's Boydton special appears to have been the source of the wire story, which ran in Washington, New York, Savannah and Raleigh on September 5 and 6. Headlines framed it as a near-lynching, such as "Want to Lynch Reprieved Negro" in the New-York Tribune, while a Mississippi paper titled it "The Law's Delays Almost Precipitates a Lynching." The Times-Dispatch headed its report "The Mob Versus the Law" yet called Bacon "the Mecklenburg murderer," and later printed the Chase City resolutions and a letter from the woman's husband arguing Bacon's guilt.

No Black-press report from September was found; the Richmond Planet printed Ferrell's letter, which called the crowd a "mob" at "fever heat," on October 3. A week later the Planet wrote that Bacon had been "sacrificed at the behest of a mob" and called the hanging "a judicial murder," asking whether Judge Homes would have insisted on it had Bacon been white.

Only the St. Louis Republic reports cries of "Lynch him!"; the wire says the crowd wanted Bacon kept at Boydton. Accounts of Finch's last words differ: the Boydton specials say he denied knowing of Bacon's part, the Times-Dispatch of September 5 says he called Bacon guilty, and the Planet says he declared him innocent.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Doc Bacon
bases: A crowd from Chase City gathered at the Boydton jail after a respite, demanded that the condemned Doc Bacon not be removed and, in one account, shouted 'Lynch him!', while an armed posse guarded him (A4, A5, A7, A17).

No one was killed: the crowd dispersed after Judge Holmes's speech and Bacon was taken away by train (A4, A5, A18), so this was a threatened lynching, not a lynching, though a large crowd acting without authority sought to keep a convicted prisoner for hanging (A3, A7).

The Richmond Times-Dispatch's local correspondent (A5, carried by the wire in A3, A4), a separate St. Louis Republic account (A7) and the Rev. J. B. Ferrell's eyewitness letter in the Richmond Planet (A16, A17) agree on the crowd at the jail, the armed guard and the judge's speech.

accounts.label: Local correspondent and wire report
accounts.gist: A large Chase City delegation at the jail demanded Bacon not be removed; an armed posse stood inside until Judge Homes/Holmes spoke for 15-20 minutes and the crowd consented to disperse.

accounts.label: St. Louis Republic dispatch
accounts.gist: A great crowd repeatedly shouted 'Lynch him!' when the stay became known and pressed around the armed officers demanding the prisoner while the judge held its attention.

accounts.label: Rev. J. B. Ferrell, eyewitness (Richmond Planet)
accounts.gist: The crowd shouted for Bacon's neck to be broken during the prayers; after the respite the 'mob' was at fever heat, the sheriff swore in about 25 armed deputies, and Bacon was slipped out a side door at twilight.

framing.detail: The Times-Dispatch headed its local report 'Mob Made Strong Demonstration' and 'The Mob Versus the Law', yet in the same piece called Bacon 'the Mecklenburg murderer'.
Northern and Southern papers ran the wire under headlines such as 'Want to Lynch Reprieved Negro', 'Negro Saved From Lynching' and 'Had Narrow Escape From Law and Mob'.
A Mississippi paper headed the condensed wire 'The Law's Delays Almost Precipitates a Lynching', placing the cause in the respite.
The Times-Dispatch printed the Chase City resolutions and the woman's husband's letter insisting on Bacon's guilt, with the warning that citizens might take the law into their own hands.
The Richmond Planet printed Ferrell's account of the crowd as a 'mob' and later called Bacon's hanging a 'judicial murder' to appease 'a howling mob'.

conflicts.note: The versions differ in intensity rather than contradicting one another; only the St. Louis Republic reports an explicit call to lynch.
The local Times-Dispatch gives the fuller name W. E. Homes; Holmes is likely a misspelling.

versions.value: Before the hanging Finch said Bacon had nothing to do with it that he knew of; on the gallows he said nothing about Bacon
On the gallows Finch recanted and declared Bacon guilty
